title: Paris from Hopewell
summary: Joseph Houston’s 1776 station near Doyle Spring grew into Hopewell, chartered in 1789 as Bourbon County’s seat, and the town was renamed Paris in 1790.
bodyMarkdown:
Paris, the seat of Bourbon County, began as a spring, a station and a town plat with a different name. Its early history is told in [Grokipedia's Paris article](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris,_Kentucky) and on [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris,_Kentucky). The two sources agree on the outline but differ on a few dates.

## Before the town

Farming peoples lived along these creeks long before Virginia surveyors arrived. Fort Ancient villages near Paris, such as the [Buckner Site](/stories/buckner-site-fort-ancient-villages-on-strodes-creek/), date to centuries before European contact. Grokipedia describes the first settler station here as a frontier outpost built "amid threats from Native American tribes."

## Houston's station

Joseph Houston, a Pennsylvanian, built a station near Doyle Spring, later called Hopewell Spring. Grokipedia dates it to 1775, and Wikipedia to 1776. Wikipedia adds that Houston was forced to move because others held earlier land grants. Other stations nearby were founded by John Hinkson, John Grant and the Ruddell brothers.

These were Virginia land claimants securing fertile Bluegrass land. One of them, Ruddell's Station, was captured by British and Shawnee forces in June 1780 ([the guns at Ruddell's Station](/stories/isaac-ruddell-and-the-guns-at-ruddells-station/)).

## A county and a county seat

Virginia created [Bourbon County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bourbon_County,_Kentucky) from Fayette County in October 1785 and named it for the French royal house, an ally in the Revolution. In 1786 Lawrence Protzman bought about 250 acres from John Reed and platted lots and streets. According to Wikipedia, he offered land for public buildings if the Virginia legislature would make his town the county seat. The first courthouse was completed in October 1787.

On September 2, 1789, the town was chartered as Hopewell. Wikipedia says Protzman named it for his hometown of Hopewell, New Jersey. In 1790 the name changed to Paris at the urging of James Garrard, who later served as a Kentucky governor. It honored the French capital and matched the county's French name.

## Bourbonton

The post office used another name for a time, Bourbonton or Bourbon Courthouse. Grokipedia says the post office opened under that name by 1794. Wikipedia places it in the early 19th century and finds no evidence that the name was ever formally applied to the town. The town was incorporated as Paris in 1839 and again in 1890.

Early Paris had grist and sawmills on Houston and Stoner Creeks, which served farmers raising hemp, tobacco and livestock. During the Civil War, Confederate raider John Hunt Morgan came through the town on July 18, 1862.

## Kentucky today

Paris had 10,171 residents at the 2020 census. The Hopewell Museum keeps the town's first name alive in a 1909 Beaux Arts building that served as the area's first post office. Duncan Tavern, a stone building from 1788, now houses a genealogical collection. Paris is a sister city of Lamotte-Beuvron in France.
